analysis.one_liner: Bans medical debt from credit reports, shortens reporting of old debts, and gives vulnerable consumers free credit monitoring.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules of consumer credit reporting. It would ban medical debt from credit reports, cut how long most negative information stays on a report (for example, bankruptcies from 10 to 7 years and collections from 7 to 4), erase paid or settled debts within 45 days, and wipe out credit damage from predatory mortgages, fraudulent for-profit-school loans, and financial abuse. It would also give free credit monitoring to people who are unemployed, on public assistance, 65 or older, active-duty military, or victims of identity theft.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with medical debt, old debts, or debts from predatory loans would see those items dropped or shortened on their credit reports, raising their scores and their access to housing, jobs, and credit. Victims of financial abuse, identity theft, and fraud would get free monitoring and easier ways to clear their records, and low-income, unemployed, and older consumers would qualify for free credit monitoring.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with medical or disputed debt

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit any information about medical debt from appearing on a consumer credit report; the bill's own findings cite CFPB research that medical collections affect nearly one in five consumers and depress credit scores even after the debt is paid.

It would shorten how long most adverse information stays on reports — bankruptcies from 10 to 7 years, collections and most other negative items from 7 to 4 — and require removal of fully paid or settled debts within 45 days.

Victims of predatory mortgage lending and servicing, and borrowers defrauded by for-profit schools, could have the resulting negative credit information removed once a court or the CFPB confirms the underlying misconduct.

Victims of financial abuse, often by a partner or family member, could submit documentation to have abuse-related debt removed without needing a police report, which the bill's findings note is often unsafe or impossible in those situations.

It would mandate free credit monitoring and identity-theft protection for fraud victims, the unemployed, public assistance recipients, active-duty military, and people 65 or older, and require a standardized affidavit so identity-theft victims don't have to navigate inconsistent paperwork.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies and debt collectors bear the cost: they lose revenue from reporting and selling credit-monitoring services, and must absorb compliance costs for faster removals. Lenders lose some visibility into borrowers' payment histories, and some of that cost could be passed back to consumers through credit pricing.

drawbacks.text: Blanket removal of accurate information — such as shortening the reporting window for bankruptcies and collections — would leave lenders with less information about a borrower's actual repayment history, which could lead to higher prices or tighter credit for some borrowers whose risk is now less visible.

Requiring removal of paid or settled debts within 45 days and processing abuse-documentation claims creates compliance burdens and dispute volume for reporting agencies and lenders, some of which could be passed to consumers through fees or credit pricing.

Several of the bill's protections depend on CFPB rulemaking — defining qualifying abuse documentation, setting 'fair and reasonable' monitoring fees, and certifying defrauded borrowers — so the real-world scope would hinge on how any future administration writes those rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for ordinary people are substantial and concrete: medical debt alone affects roughly one in five consumers' reports, and the bill targets several groups — abuse survivors, fraud victims, defrauded students — for whom credit damage blocks housing, jobs, and independence. The main cost falls on credit bureaus and collectors rather than the public, though there is a real trade-off: erasing accurate negative information faster does remove risk signals lenders use, which could mean somewhat higher credit prices or tighter lending for borderline borrowers. Weighing them honestly, the public benefit outweighs the cost, which is largely borne by the industries being regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote before Congress's term ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on August 8, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill's support was narrow: one sponsor and four cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The three nationwide credit bureaus, debt buyers and collectors, and other companies whose reporting and monitoring revenue the bill would have cut are better off because it died. Consumers with medical or erroneous debt on their reports see no change.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would ban medical debt from credit reports, shorten how long most negative information stays on reports, and mandate free credit monitoring for vulnerable consumers.

for.name: Four House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and no hearing, markup, or vote ever took place before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's five House sponsors were all Democrats, so the partisan shape beyond that is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would bar the bureaus from reporting medical debt and much other adverse information, force removal of paid debts within 45 days, and cut into their credit-monitoring business by mandating free monitoring for vulnerable consumers.
The bill would shorten how long collections stay on reports to four years and require removal of paid or settled debts within 45 days, shrinking the leverage collectors gain from reporting debts.
Borrowers defrauded by for-profit schools could have adverse information from their private loans removed, eliminating a collection channel these lenders rely on.

Students defrauded by proprietary schools could get their loan information stripped from credit reports, removing a tool that keeps former students on the hook for debts from programs that misled them.

The bill would require bureaus to provide free credit monitoring to fraud victims, the unemployed, public assistance recipients, seniors 65 and over, and servicemembers, undercutting paid subscriptions for exactly these groups.
